Day-to-Day Startup

After the first time, most of the setup checklist is already done and stays done.

The named volume from docker-compose.yml (containerized MySQL topic) means your database's data survives the container stopping — it's stored on disk, not inside the container itself. That makes ordinary day-to-day startup much shorter than the first-time checklist:

docker compose up -d mysql
npm run dev

No migration and no reseed needed — the tables and the data from last time are both still there. Re-run docker compose up -d mysql any time you're not sure whether the container is running; Docker Compose simply does nothing if it's already up, rather than erroring or restarting it. The only time you'd go back to the fuller first-time checklist is starting again from a genuinely empty database — for instance, docker compose down -v (-v removes the named volume too, deleting all the data with it) if you ever want a clean slate.
